notes: TERMINAL STATE IS PARTIAL AND THE TWO UNMET GATES ARE NAMED. This is the outcome the parent predicted in the dispatch brief, and the node did not weaken anything to avoid it.

GATE 1, ACCEPTED ModelCommit, REFUSED ON VOLUME AFTER THE COHORT WAS REPAIRED. The refusal used to be `degenerate_axis`: every holdout decision succeeded on its first attempt, so each carried a candidate axis of arity 1, which cannot be ranked, and 7D's attribution refused before the decision floor was reached. That was a fixture defect with two causes, both measured before anything was edited. The `flaky` models were registered at priority 20 while every healthy model sat at 10, and `router::order` sorts on priority ascending, so routing could never select them and their injected 500 never fired. And the odd/even failure rule could not admit a measurable cohort at ANY window size: the plan head is attempted exactly once per decision, so an odd/even head answers on every even ask, which measured 16 rankable and 14 degenerate at a 53.3% failover rate, and `measure_release_evidence` aborts the whole partition on the FIRST arity-1 decision. The injected models now fail every call, which is what the mechanism's own doc comment always claimed and the code never did. The K axis is now `arity 2: 30` with zero degenerate, and the refusal is `sample_too_small`: 12 effective holdout decisions against a floor of 30.

NOTHING WAS LOWERED TO OBTAIN THAT NUMBER, and this is the part that makes the refusal trustworthy. `min_decisions` stays 30, `minimum_effect` stays 0.05, `alpha` stays 0.05, `power` stays 0.80, the tripwire still asserts `StatisticalConfig::default()` verbatim and still prints 314, 785 and 1570, no sample was synthesised, and the window was NOT enlarged to clear a floor it was one request short of. The parent confirmed by blob hash that `ml/statistics.rs`, `ml/offline_gate.rs`, `ml/calibration.rs`, `ml/dataset.rs` and the boundary test are byte-identical to the pre-repair commit.

THE WINDOW IS A REPRESENTATIVE FIXTURE AND NOT A REPRESENTATIVE FLEET, and the fixture says so itself in `FAILOVER_FRACTION`. The 100% first-choice failure rate was CHOSEN and is not plausible as a production failure rate; it is forced by the gate's all-or-nothing arity requirement, and the entry lists what the window CAN support (that the gate can walk a cohort whose decisions genuinely contained a choice) separately from what it CANNOT (anything about production failure rates, or about router behaviour when upstream failures are rare). There is a SECOND independent axis of unrepresentativeness, added after the parent caught its absence: the fixture raises both circuit-breaker thresholds so nothing is quarantined mid-window, so the breaker can never open and the regime the window describes could not survive a few dozen requests in production. A reader must not read the breaker never firing as a finding about health tracking.

A STALE COMMENT IN THE REPAIR WAS CAUGHT BY THE PARENT AND CORRECTED. The repair's own documentation claimed the axis was 'deliberately not uniform' while its test printed `arity 2: 30`, which is uniform; it was a survivor from the earlier odd/even iteration. It was fixed rather than merged with a note, because this node's headline defect was a doc comment asserting a behaviour the code did not have, and a passing comment is not evidence while the printed histogram is.

Everything else in gate 1 passed and is worth stating because it is real: replay 30 of 30 bit-identical, terminal agreements 30 of 30, retention load-bearing on 120 of 240 feature positions, 30 served identities, a 30-decision holdout with 0 overlap against the fit set, calibration calibrated, the commit's plain-JSON transport exact with 0 of 167 parameters moved, and the float round trip exact at max 0 ulp. The float constituent's field count rose from 211 to 361 across the fixture repair and that is EXPECTED rather than a regression: it counts f64 fields per sample across the sample set pushed through the transport, and a decision that fails over contributes two attempt-scope rows instead of one, so the measured sample set grew from roughly 35 to roughly 60. The transported artifact did not change.

THE SHADOW DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT IS SERVED, and this was measured rather than asserted. Four windows with a fresh AppState and a fresh fake upstream each, same 34-request sequence: one attached, and two candidate-withdrawn runs as a control. The differences between the attached run and the control are exactly the control's own differences, which is none. Bodies were compared byte for byte with 0 of 34 ids masked; the only field excluded anywhere is hyper's clock-derived Date header.

THE COMPARISON IS A MEASUREMENT AND NOT A TAUTOLOGY, which is what makes the point above worth anything: 30 of 30 shadow records changed their commit and decision checksum between the withdrawn and attached runs while 0 served bytes changed. A separate assertion fails the build if the candidate ever IS the cold-start commit, because that would make the whole comparison vacuous.

ROLLBACK is demonstrated before, during and after rather than described. Two servers in lockstep with separate fake upstreams, so the comparison never measures the router's own evolving latency state: window 1 before withdrawal was identical across both, the withdrawal is one-way and idempotent, and window 2 after was identical again. The worker reports that its first attempt DID report differences and that the cause was its own measurement error, not the shadow; comparing one server's window 1 against its own window 2 measures the router's latency drift. That correction is the useful part of the evidence.

NO PRODUCTION TRAFFIC EXISTS AND THE RECORDS SAY SO. Every artifact, comment and claim says real requests through the production serving path against a LOCAL FAKE UPSTREAM. The forbidden phrases real traffic, production traffic and live traffic appear nowhere except inside the negative assertion that forbids them.

THE WORKER REPORTED ONE FAILING TEST AND THERE WERE THREE. cargo test aborts at the first failing test binary, so the e2e failure masked two more that appeared only after it was fixed, and several gates the report described as passing had in fact never run to completion. The parent found them, fixed them as fixture corrections, and verified each still fails when it should; see E-103.

THE SERVING PATH IS REACHED THREE TIMES AND THE COUNT IS RECORDED DIFFERENTLY NOW. 7F moved the evaluation reach behind one AppState hop so the predictor never leaves AppState, which is why the source counts read 2, 4 and 2 rather than 3, 3 and 2. An exact source-text count is brittle by construction; the forbidden-token scan over the four marked shadow blocks is the load-bearing assertion in that test, and the counts are secondary.

A KNOWN IMPRECISION, recorded rather than left for someone to discover: the server passes the candidate to `evaluate_with` per call, so `ShadowEngine`'s own internally pinned predictor is still genesis. `predictor_commit()` therefore describes what that engine would use on its own, not what production used. Nothing depends on it being otherwise today, and the per-call design is what keeps the predictor from being reachable at all.

Reachability is proven by a diagnostic log line rather than an endpoint, on purpose: an endpoint would be a new capability rather than evidence about an existing one. No activation, no swap, no try_train, no takeover, no exploration, no runtime training, no new dependency, no endpoint, no UI change, and no claim that the model is safe to serve.
